e-5908.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector With Respect to a Given Inner Product
e-5908.problem:
An inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  2x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + 3x_3 y_3.$ 
Calculate the norm of the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14057327/assets/1e710ca7b3b7bea626de36181a30869b0f114a4497843c6b6ea8b8966a91d208.png) under this inner product.
e-5908.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $\mathbf v$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\|\mathbf{v}\|$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{2\cdot (3\cdot 3)+2\cdot 2+3\cdot (1\cdot 1)} \\  & =\sqrt{18+4+3} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

e-5548.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Polynomials
e-5548.problem:
Let $V=\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle {x}(t), {y}(t) \rangle = x(1)y(1) + x(2)y(2) + x(3)y(3).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector  $p(t) = 1 - t^2.$
e-5548.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${p}(t) = 1-t^2,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=0,\qquad 
p(2)= -3,\qquad 
p(3)=-8.
$$

Computing $\|p(t)\|$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(1)p(1)+p(2)p(2)+p(3)p(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+9+64} \\  & =\sqrt{73}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-5549.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
e-5549.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,1\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)= 2t-1.$
e-5549.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle  f(t),  f(t) \rangle}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}-2{t}^{2}+t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-2+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}.
$$

e-5550.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
e-5550.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,\pi\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,\pi\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)= 3t.$
e-5550.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle  f(t),  f(t) \rangle}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }9{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =3{\pi }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| f(t) \|  = \sqrt{3\pi^3} = \pi \sqrt{3\pi}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $\| f(t) \| \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{3\pi }}\cdot 3t \\  & =\frac{t\sqrt{3}}{\pi \sqrt{\pi }}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector With Respect to a Given Inner Product
content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 
Calculate the norm of the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $‖v‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot (-2\cdot (-2))+2\cdot (0\cdot 0)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+12+0} \\  & =\sqrt{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 
Calculate the norm of the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $‖v‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{2\cdot 2+2\cdot ((-1)\cdot (-1))+4\cdot 4} \\  & =\sqrt{4+2+16} \\  & =\sqrt{22}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(0)y(0)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $p(t)=4-2t+{t}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=4-2t+{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(0)=4,\,p(2)=4,\,p(3)=7.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(0)p(0)+p(2)p(2)+p(3)p(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(0)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(7)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+16+49} \\  & =\sqrt{81} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(\frac{2\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi }{4})-(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4}) \\  & =(\pi +0)-(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Let V=C[π,2π] be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on [π,2π], equipped with the inner product

⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=∫π2πx(t)y(t)dt.

Calculate the norm of the vector f(t)=cos⁡t.

a
π
b
0
c
2π
d
3π2
e
π2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector f(t) with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as

‖f(t)‖=⟨f(t),f(t)⟩.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨f(t),f(t)⟩=∫π2π(f(t))2dt=∫π2πcos2⁡tdt=∫π2π(1+cos⁡2t2)dt=∫π2π(12+cos⁡2t2)dt=(t2+sin⁡2t4)|π2π=(2π2+sin⁡4π4)−(π2+sin⁡2π4)=(π+0)−(π2+0)=π2.

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity

cos2⁡t=1+cos⁡2t2.

Finally then,

‖f(t)‖=π2.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms that the squared norm is \int_{\pi}^{2\pi}\cos^2(t)\,dt=\pi/2. Taking its square root gives \sqrt{\pi/2}, option e.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
content.problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(\frac{2\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi }{4})-(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4}) \\  & =(\pi +0)-(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Let V=C[0,4] be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on [0,4], equipped with the inner product

⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=∫04x(t)y(t)dt.

Calculate the norm of the vector f(t)=t+1.

a
 563
b
 683
c
 343
d
 23
e
 323
Submit

decision.explanation: The squared norm is \int_0^4(\sqrt{t}+1)^2\,dt=\int_0^4(t+2\sqrt{t}+1)\,dt=[t^2/2+(4/3)t^{3/2}+t]_0^4=8+32/3+4=68/3. Therefore the norm is \sqrt{68/3}.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Let $V=C[0,4]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,4],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{4}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\sqrt{t}+1.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(\sqrt{t}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t+2\sqrt{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{4t\sqrt{t}}{3}+t)|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =(8+\frac{32}{3}+4) \\  & =\frac{68}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{68}{3}}.
$$

EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector f(t) with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as

‖f(t)‖=⟨f(t),f(t)⟩.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨f(t),f(t)⟩=∫04(f(t))2dt=∫04(t+1)2dt=∫04(t+2t+1)dt=(t22+4tt3+t)|04=(8+323+4)=683.

‖f(t)‖=683.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
content.problem:
Let $V=C[0,4]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,4],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{4}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\sqrt{t}+1.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(\sqrt{t}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t+2\sqrt{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{4t\sqrt{t}}{3}+t)|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =(8+\frac{32}{3}+4) \\  & =\frac{68}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{68}{3}}.
$$

decision.explanation: The squared norm is \int_0^1(2t+\sqrt{t})^2\,dt=\int_0^1(4t^2+4t^{3/2}+t)\,dt=4/3+8/5+1/2=103/30. Hence the norm is \sqrt{103/30}.

after.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=2t+\sqrt{t}.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+\sqrt{t})^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+4t\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{8{t}^{2}\sqrt{t}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+\frac{8}{5}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{103}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{103}{30}}.
$$

content.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=2t+\sqrt{t}.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+\sqrt{t})^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+4t\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{8{t}^{2}\sqrt{t}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+\frac{8}{5}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{103}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{103}{30}}.
$$

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\,{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4})-(-\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{4}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}

$$

$$

decision.explanation: The squared norm is \int_{-1}^{1}(1-t)^2\,dt=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-2t+t^2)\,dt=2+2/3=8/3. Thus the norm is \sqrt{8/3}=2\sqrt{2/3}.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=1-t.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-t)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-{t}^{2}+t)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1+1)-(\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}-(-1)^{2}+(-1)) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.
$$

Question 16
?

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=3x1y1+x2y2+3x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[2−11] under this inner product.

a
14[2−11]
b
66[2−11]
c
22[2−11]
d
24[2−11]
e
1111[2−11]
Submit

decision.explanation: The norm is \|v\|=\sqrt{3(2^2)+(-1)^2+3(1^2)}=\sqrt{16}=4. Dividing v by 4 gives the normalized vector.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩=3{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =3\cdot (2\cdot 2)+(-1)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot (1\cdot 1) \\  & =12+1+3 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{16}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=3x1y1+x2y2+3x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[2−11] under this inner product.

a
14[2−11]
b
66[2−11]
c
22[2−11]
d
24[2−11]
e
1111[2−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector v with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as

‖v‖=⟨v,v⟩.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨v,v⟩=3⋅(2⋅2)+(−1)⋅(−1)+3⋅(1⋅1)=12+1+3=16.

Therefore,

‖v‖=16=4.

To normalize the vector v, we divide v by its norm ‖v‖:

u=v‖v‖=14[2−11]

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩=3{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =3\cdot (2\cdot 2)+(-1)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot (1\cdot 1) \\  & =12+1+3 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{16}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)=t-1.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{(t-1)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-{t}^{2}+t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-1+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
‖f(t)‖=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $‖f(t)‖:$

$$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)=t-1.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{(t-1)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-{t}^{2}+t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-1+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
‖f(t)‖=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $‖f(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{t-1}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(t-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=2x1y1+2x2y2+x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[32−3] under this inner product.

a
3535[32−3]
b
122[32−3]
c
22[32−3]
d
2222[32−3]
e
77[32−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: The norm is \|v\|=\sqrt{2(3^2)+2(2^2)+(-3)^2}=\sqrt{35}. Normalize by dividing v by \sqrt{35}; since 1/\sqrt{35}=\sqrt{35}/35, option a is correct.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot (3\cdot 3)+2\cdot (2\cdot 2)+(-3)\cdot (-3) \\  & =18+8+9 \\  & =35.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{35}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{35}}{35}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=2x1y1+2x2y2+x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[32−3] under this inner product.

a
3535[32−3]
b
122[32−3]
c
22[32−3]
d
2222[32−3]
e
77[32−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector v with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as

‖v‖=⟨v,v⟩.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨v,v⟩=2⋅(3⋅3)+2⋅(2⋅2)+(−3)⋅(−3)=18+8+9=35.

Therefore,

‖v‖=35.

To normalize the vector v, we divide v by its norm ‖v‖:

u=v‖v‖=135[32−3]=3535[32−3]

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot (3\cdot 3)+2\cdot (2\cdot 2)+(-3)\cdot (-3) \\  & =18+8+9 \\  & =35.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{35}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{35}}{35}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $1,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2).
$$

Normalize the  vector  $p(t)=2+t.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.
$$

Since $p(t)=2+t,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=3,\,p(2)=4.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),p(t)⟩ & =[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =9+16 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{25}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $p(t)$, we divide $p(t)$ by its norm $‖p(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{p(t)}{‖p(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{2+t}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2+t)\end{aligned}
$$

Let V=R1[t] be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most 1, equipped with the inner product ⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2). Normalize the vector p(t)=2+t.

a
15(2+t)
b
1050(2+t)
c
5(2+t)
d
2(2+t)
e
12(2+t)
Submit

EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector f(t) with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as ‖p(t)‖=⟨p(t),p(t)⟩.

Since p(t)=2+t, we obtain

p(1)=3,p(2)=4.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨p(t),p(t)⟩=[p(1)]2+[p(2)]2=32+42=9+16=25.

Therefore,

‖p(t)‖=25=5.

To normalize the vector p(t), we divide p(t) by its norm ‖p(t)‖:

u(t)=p(t)‖p(t)‖=2+t5=15(2+t)

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms p(1)=3 and p(2)=4, giving norm \sqrt{9+16}=5. Dividing p(t) by 5 yields \frac{1}{5}(2+t), option a.

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $1,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2).
$$

Normalize the  vector  $p(t)=2+t.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.
$$

Since $p(t)=2+t,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=3,\,p(2)=4.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),p(t)⟩ & =[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =9+16 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{25}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $p(t)$, we divide $p(t)$ by its norm $‖p(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{p(t)}{‖p(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{2+t}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2+t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20
?

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+3x2y2+x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[21−1] under this inner product.

a
12[21−1]
b
36[21−1]
c
33[21−1]
d
24[21−1]
e
22[21−1]
Submit

decision.explanation: The norm is \|v\|=\sqrt{2^2+3(1^2)+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}. Dividing v by this norm gives the coefficient 1/(2\sqrt{2})=\sqrt{2}/4, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

An inner product on V=R3 is defined as ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+3x2y2+x3y3.

Normalize the vector v=[21−1] under this inner product.

a
12[21−1]
b
36[21−1]
c
33[21−1]
d
24[21−1]
e
22[21−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The norm of a vector v with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is defined as

‖v‖=⟨v,v⟩.

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

⟨v,v⟩=2⋅2+3⋅1⋅1+(−1)⋅(−1)=4+3+1=8.

Therefore,

‖v‖=8=22.

To normalize the vector v, we divide v by its norm ‖v‖:

u=v‖v‖=122[21−1]=24[21−1]

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
